sources.title: Towards Accurate Generative Models of Video: A New Metric & Challenges

B. SCV Data Generation; B.1. Scenario Parameters
D. Examples of Video Models on SCV
omissions: Text extraction does not reconstruct figure images; inspect the retained PDF for figures and equation/table layout.
Separate supplemental material availability has not been fully verified.

The extraction limitation was addressed by visually inspecting every page of the supplied 17-page PDF, including all figures and tables. Separate supplements, linked code, pretrained weights and dataset files were not inspected; no experiments were reproduced.

Version scope: the supplied title page identifies arXiv:1812.01717v2 [cs.CV], 27 March 2019. The catalog records the original 3 December 2018 submission and 2018 publication year. Title and all six authors agree, with Raphaël rendered without its accent in the catalog. The original v1 was not supplied, so revision contents were not compared.

synopsis: Fréchet Video Distance (FVD) compares distributions of real and generated videos using pretrained action-recognition features and Gaussian statistics. The paper validates sensitivity to temporal corruption and agreement with human preferences, then introduces StarCraft 2 Videos (SCV) to expose failures in motion, interaction and memory. Its central tradeoff is a useful distribution-level score whose interpretation depends on the embedding, sample count and evaluation protocol.

problem.text: Framewise PSNR and SSIM compare a prediction against a particular reference, which penalizes alternative plausible futures and does not directly evaluate a distribution of videos. The authors seek an evaluation that includes appearance, temporal coherence and diversity, alongside controllable scenarios that reveal failures hidden by visually complicated real-world data.

contributions.text: FVD replaces image features with video features. The paper compares embedding layers, pretraining datasets and a kernel-distance alternative, then evaluates corruption sensitivity and human agreement.

SCV supplies four adjustable game scenarios: Move Unit to Border (MUtB), Collect Mineral Shards (CMS), Brawl and Road Trip with Medivac (RTwM). Baselines make these challenges concrete without introducing a new video generator.

inputs: Samples of real RGB videos and generated RGB videos; conditional evaluations concatenate context with predicted frames.
outputs: One distribution-level FVD score; lower is better. No actions or individual-video correctness certificates are produced.

steps.name: Embed entire clips
steps.detail: Apply a pretrained Inflated 3D Convnet (I3D) to each video. Candidate representations are final logits and last-pooling outputs from RGB Kinetics-400 or Kinetics-600 models. Subsequent experiments select Kinetics-400 logits following the diagnostic comparison.

steps.name: Estimate two feature distributions
steps.detail: Fit a multivariate Gaussian to each set of embeddings, estimating its mean and covariance. Compute the Gaussian Fréchet expression below. The Gaussian approximation occurs in learned feature space; it is not a claim that raw videos are Gaussian.

steps.name: Separate alternative metrics
steps.detail: Kernel Video Distance (KVD) instead uses a polynomial-kernel MMD estimator on I3D features. The image baseline averages Inception frame features, or frame-feature differences, before applying the same Gaussian distance. These alternatives test the distance and representation choices.

steps.name: Construct controlled video challenges
steps.detail: Deterministic SC2LE agents create replays with scenario-controlled randomness, then render the same states at different resolutions. Right-click cues are visible in the videos. Each scenario supplies 10,000 training, 2,000 validation and 2,000 test videos.

training.text: FVD uses already pretrained action-recognition features; this paper does not train a new FVD-specific generator or control policy. Separately, CDNA, SV2P, SVP-FP and SAVP are trained as evaluation subjects using Tensor2Tensor implementations.

Baselines receive 300,000 updates. The learning-rate grid is 10^{-3}, 10^{-4}, 10^{-5}; VAE models vary the reconstruction/KL tradeoff, SV2P uses the cited annealing schedule, and SAVP additionally tunes GAN and GAN-VAE loss weights. The printed KL-weight grid is ambiguous, as recorded below.

inference.text: Evaluation embeds completed videos and compares aggregate statistics; it does not run feedback control. BAIR, MUtB, CMS and Brawl use two context plus fourteen predicted frames; KTH uses ten plus ten. FVD evaluation uses 256 validation samples for BAIR and 1,024 for KTH/SCV. SCV clips begin at frame zero; BAIR/KTH use consecutive subsequences. RTwM's horizon is inconsistent between body and appendix.

equations.explanation: Equation (2): μ_R and μ_G are real and generated feature means; Σ_R and Σ_G are their covariance matrices. The mean term compares feature centers and the trace term compares covariance structure. Lower values indicate closer fitted distributions. The score has feature-dependent scale, rather than percentage units, and finite-sample estimates can be positive even for identical underlying distributions.

results.task: Human agreement when PSNR cannot distinguish models
results.setting: BAIR; ten models selected to have equal PSNR near the best quartile. Three generated videos per selected model; pairwise ratings by two raters, with a third resolving disagreement.
results.comparison: KVD: 73.8%; averaged FID: 52.0%; SSIM: 44.6%; agreement among raters: 84.4%.
results.interpretation: Supports discrimination among models tied by PSNR under this selection protocol. PSNR/SSIM selection uses the best frame-averaged score among 100 generations per context; FVD uses distribution statistics.

results.setting: Two context frames plus fourteen outputs; 256 validation samples for FVD.
results.interpretation: SAVP leads this benchmark column. These are reported point estimates without table-level uncertainty or action-execution evaluation.

results.setting: SCV-MUtB; two context plus fourteen output frames; 1,024 evaluation samples.
results.interpretation: The ranking differs from BAIR, illustrating why a single benchmark winner cannot be assumed across scenarios.

results.setting: SCV-RTwM; 1,024 evaluation samples; two context frames, with unresolved total/output-length wording.
results.interpretation: The numerical winner is not a successful memory model: the authors report that all evaluated models fail RTwM. No scenario-success rate is supplied.

results.setting: BAIR comparisons around base scores 200 and 400; 1,800 video comparisons.
results.metric: Human agreement as FVD difference increases
results.value: Authors interpret differences of about 50 points or more as typically perceptible.
results.comparison: Smaller differences are described as near chance; Figure 5 plots standard errors and counts similar-quality judgments as disagreement.
results.interpretation: A study-specific calibration, not a universal significance threshold. The plotted base-200 curve includes a point below 0.5 despite the prose's 'never worse' qualification.

limitations.text: The human study is on BAIR and selected model families. Table 1 does not show universal dominance: averaged FID exceeds FVD for spread-SSIM selections (62.7% versus 58.4%), and KVD narrowly exceeds it for spread-PSNR (63.8% versus 63.5%). Generalization to other video domains remains unestablished here.

FVD depends on the pretrained representation and a Gaussian approximation. It measures video distributions, not whether each conditional prediction follows its own context. Concatenating context can expose switching, but does not establish a guarantee of conditional correctness or control competence.

Finite-sample FVD is positively biased even for two subsets of the same BAIR distribution. Figure 4 reports small standard errors across 50 trials at fixed sample size; that repeatability does not remove bias. Compare scores using matched sample counts.

SCV sacrifices real-world visual fidelity for controllable interactions. The reported CMS disappearance errors, Brawl blurring and RTwM failures motivate semantic diagnostics, but the paper leaves RTwM's failure cause—longer horizon versus scenario complexity—unresolved.

reproduction.text: Use the specified I3D feature choice, matched clip construction and sample counts, and the SCV split/rendering protocol. Appendix B skips the first two rendered frames and records every sixth frame for MUtB, fourth for CMS/Brawl and eighth for RTwM. The introduction reports over 100 GPU-years overall. Code and pretrained-weight links are claims of availability, not verification. Exact software/checkpoint versions, batch size and GPU model/count are not specified in the supplied implementation description.

Preserve unresolved source details: Appendix C prints β = (10^{-6}, 10^{-5}, 10^{-6}, 10^{-3}), repeating 10^{-6}; do not silently replace it. Section 4.4 says two context frames plus up to 32 additional RTwM frames, whereas Appendix B says exactly 32 frames total. The KVD formula also prints j ≠ j under its final sum. These require clarification before an exact implementation claim.

reasoning.text: The recorded metrics classification is supported: the contribution evaluates video distributions and introduces a benchmark. Pretrained I3D action recognition supplies features; deterministic agents collect SCV videos. Neither constitutes a proposed action-generating world model, so architecture, prediction-paradigm and quadrant labels remain not applicable.

discussionQuestions: How much can FVD improve while SCV entity identity, collection order or cargo consistency remains wrong?
Would the approximately 50-point perceptual separation persist after changing the dataset, sample count or I3D representation?

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title/author block, equal-contribution footnote and arXiv margin
evidence.detail: The title matches the manifest. The six authors are Thomas Unterthiner, Sjoerd van Steenkiste, Karol Kurach, Raphaël Marinier, Marcin Michalski and Sylvain Gelly. Affiliations are Johannes Kepler University; IDSIA, SUPSI, USI; and Google Brain. The margin identifies v2, 27 March 2019.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 1–2, Abstract and Section 1 contributions
evidence.detail: Motivates temporal coherence, appearance and diversity evaluation and introduces FVD plus SCV. The final contribution bullet reports over 100 GPU-years of experiments.

evidence.location: PDF p. 2, Section 2, Equations (1)–(2) and following paragraph
evidence.detail: Defines the Gaussian Fréchet expression using means and covariances and motivates fitting distributions in learned feature space.

evidence.location: PDF p. 3, Section 2, I3D paragraphs; p. 6, Section 4.1, embedding choice
evidence.detail: Compares RGB Kinetics-400/600 I3D logits and pooling features; selects Kinetics-400 logits for subsequent FVD experiments.

evidence.location: PDF p. 3, Section 2, MMD formula and polynomial-kernel paragraph
evidence.detail: KVD uses MMD with kernel k(a,b) = (a^T b + 1)^3. The printed last summation condition is j ≠ j, an unresolved typographical defect.

evidence.location: PDF p. 3, Section 2, comparison with PSNR/SSIM
evidence.detail: FVD evaluates distributions and can include context plus generated frames to detect switching; it supports unconditional evaluation without paired target sequences.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 4–5, Figure 2 and Section 3 scenario descriptions
evidence.detail: Defines MUtB motion, CMS collection, Brawl interactions and RTwM pickup/transport/unloading consistency; discusses the visual-fidelity tradeoff.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Figure 3 and Section 4.1; p. 6, Section 4.1
evidence.detail: Tests four static and four temporal corruptions on BAIR, Kinetics and HMDB51, comparing I3D variants and averaged image-feature baselines.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section 4.2 and Figure 4
evidence.detail: Non-overlapping BAIR subsets produce positive FVD at finite sample sizes; the curve spans 2^5–2^12 samples and error bars are standard errors over 50 trials.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 6–7, Section 4.3, model selection and Set-up
evidence.detail: BAIR study uses four model families, two context plus fourteen output frames, 256 unseen reference videos, best-of-100 PSNR/SSIM, ten-model equal/spread selections and three displayed videos per selected model.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Table 1, FVD/KVD/Avg. FID/SSIM and Among raters rows; eq. PSNR, spr. FVD, spr. SSIM and spr. PSNR columns
evidence.detail: Equal-PSNR agreement is 81.0% FVD, 73.8% KVD, 52.0% averaged FID, 44.6% SSIM and 84.4% among raters. Spread-FVD agreement is 71.9% for FVD. Spread-SSIM favors averaged FID 62.7% over FVD 58.4%; spread-PSNR favors KVD 63.8% over FVD 63.5%.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Section 4.3.1; p. 8, Figure 5 and caption
evidence.detail: Uses base FVD 200/400 and 1,800 comparisons to interpret perceptual separations near 50 points. Ties count against agreement; error bars are standard errors. The base-200 curve has a sub-0.5 point despite the textual 'never worse' statement.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Section 4.4, evaluation protocol paragraph
evidence.detail: Specifies context/output horizons, BAIR's 256 and KTH/SCV's 1,024 evaluation samples, clip selection and the two-context-plus-up-to-32-output RTwM wording.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Table 2, all model rows; BAIR, KTH and paired SCV-resolution columns
evidence.detail: Reports FVD for CDNA, SV2P, SVP-FP and SAVP. SCV left/right entries are 64 × 64/128 × 128. SAVP has BAIR 116.4 and KTH 78.0; CDNA has MUtB-128 51.4; SV2P has RTwM-128 1026.1. The table supplies no uncertainty.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Section 4.4 qualitative discussion; pp. 14–17, Appendix D, Figures 7–10
evidence.detail: Discusses disappearing units, incorrect CMS collection sequences, blurry Brawl groups and RTwM failure. Appendix images order rows as reference, CDNA, SV2P, SVP-FP, SAVP.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Section 4.5
evidence.detail: Reports weaker correlation of FVD with PSNR than with SSIM, over the collection of model configurations used for the final correlation experiment.

evidence.location: PDF p. 11, Appendix A and Table 3
evidence.detail: Uses 90% of available train/test samples for corruption diagnostics. Maps intensities to parameters, including 4–24 local/global swaps, 2–6 interleaved sequences and switching after 1–5 frames.

evidence.location: PDF p. 11, Figure 6, legend and eight noise-type groups
evidence.detail: Spearman correlations compare four FVD and four KVD embeddings plus two FID baselines. Kinetics-400 logits is competitive but not highest in every corruption group.

evidence.location: PDF p. 12, Appendix B and Table 4
evidence.detail: Gives 10,000/2,000/2,000 training/validation/test videos per scenario, deterministic agents, visual click cues, replay rendering, sampling strides, initialization-frame skipping and exactly 32 RTwM frames.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 12–13, Appendix B.1, scenario parameter paragraphs
evidence.detail: Default CMS uses two marines and 20 shards; Brawl uses nine units per army with randomized sides; RTwM has one to four units and two beacons.

evidence.location: PDF p. 13, Appendix C, complete paragraph
evidence.detail: States Tensor2Tensor implementations, default parameters, learning-rate grid, the duplicated β-grid entry, SV2P annealing, SAVP loss tuning between 10^{-6} and 10^{-3}, and 300,000 updates.

evidence.location: PDF p. 2, contribution footnotes; p. 3, footnote 4
evidence.detail: Provides links described as FVD code, SCV data and pretrained I3D weights; these links do not establish inspected or reproduced implementations.
